# Good Data Management

Good data management is essential for reliable, reproducible, and
compliant research. At the RIVM, all data work should begin with a solid
DMP, which provides a framework for organizing, storing, and maintaining
data responsibly throughout the project and data life cycle.

Please note: This section explains general rules for good data management
that are meant for everyone at RIVM.  For more practical advice or tips
that fit your own team or department, please check the agreements and
documents used in your group.  These local guidelines often have more
specific recommendations for your daily work.

## Data Organization and Structure

### Folder Structure

A clear and consistent 📁 folder structure is essential for organizing
your project and making it understandable for both yourself and
collaborators. Most reproducible research guides recommend a structure
that separates raw data, processed data, scripts, and documentation,
such as:

```         
/project-root
  /data
    /raw
    /processed
  /scripts
  /docs
```

This example is widely recognized and provides an intuitive overview
of the main project components. However, it's important to consider
how data management interacts with version control. If your project
is tracked using Git, as recommended in @sec-versioncontrol
you should avoid adding large datasets, especially raw data,
directly to your repository. Instead, store data in a dedicated database,
data management system (DMS), or a secure network location (e.g., R:
or S: drive). If you need to work with local copies, keep them in a
separate project folder (such as ./data), and ensure that these files
are excluded from version control using .gitignore.

Another consideration is the /processed folder. If your analyses and
transformations are fully reproducible, processed data can be generated
on demand and may not need to be stored permanently. In this case,
the folder can serve as a temporary workspace or cache, rather than a
repository of final results.

Given these nuances, we suggest two approaches:

1.  Standardized outline for publications:
    For projects intended for publication or broader sharing
    (such as open source releases), we recommend adopting the RIVM
    [template-scientific-repo](https://github.com/rivm-syso/Template-scientific-repo)
    folder structure. This template provides a well-organized framework
    for managing scientific modelling projects, especially those meant
    for production, collaboration, or future publication. It embodies best
    practices for clarity, reproducibility, and maintainability, and aligns
    with RIVM guidelines for publishing repositories. The template serves as
    a robust starting point, while you are free to expand and customize within
    your project, the base structure ensures your repository remains suitable
    for open publication and sharing. Importantly, it separates code from
    data, encouraging you to keep datasets outside the code repository and,
    when possible, publish them in dedicated data repositories for greater
    openness and compliance.

2. Custom Structure:
    Alternatively, you may opt for a custom folder structure tailored to the
    unique needs of your project and team. This approach is especially useful
    for complex workflows or when specific requirements must be met, such
    as mandatory structures for programming language packages, registration
    processes, or cases where only a portion of the code or data can be made
    publicly available due to security or privacy concerns. When designing
    a custom structure, prioritize clarity, reproducibility, and effective
    collaboration: handle data thoughtfully, keep scripts and documentation
    organized, and clearly communicate where files are stored and how they
    are accessed. Always document your structure in the project README so
    that collaborators and future users can easily navigate your project.

By choosing the structure that best fits your goals, whether standardized
for publication or customized for specialized workflows, you support both
open science and the practical needs of your research. Separating code
and data not only makes open publication easier, but also enables you
to publish datasets in appropriate data repositories, further increasing
transparency and impact.

### File Naming Conventions

Consistent and descriptive file names make it easier to find, organize,
and track files throughout your project 🏷️.

- Use clear and meaningful names that reflect the content and purpose
  of the file (e.g., airquality_data.csv). 
- Avoid spaces, special characters, and ambiguous abbreviations. Use
  underscores _ or hyphens - to separate words.  
- Document your naming convention in the project README so everyone
  follows the same system.

### Metadata and Documentation

Metadata and documentation help others understand your data and its context.

- Add a README file to each folder explaining its contents and purpose.
- Use standardized metadata formats (such as Dublin Core or other metadata standard) to describe datasets: who collected the data, when, how, and what it contains.
- Keep documentation up to date as your data or project changes.

## Data Storage and Backup

### Storage Options 💾

Choose secure, approved storage solutions to protect data and ensure accessibility.

- Store data on network drives or approved cloud platforms.
- Avoid using personal computers or local drives for sensitive or critical data.
- (If possible) Use a Data Management System like iRODS

### Backups 🔄

Backups protect against data loss from accidents or technical issues.

- Set up automatic, scheduled backups for all important data.
- Store backups in a secure location, separate from the original data.
- Test backup recovery procedures regularly to make sure you can restore data if needed.

### Data Security 🔒

Keep data safe by controlling access and protecting sensitive information.

- Restrict access to files based on team roles and responsibilities.
- Use strong passwords and two-factor authentication for data systems when available.
- Encrypt sensitive data, especially when storing or transferring outside RIVM secure environment.
- Keep a record of who has access to which data.

## Data Quality Assurance

Ensuring data quality is essential for robust, reproducible research. Good
data quality assurance covers validation, documentation and provenance,
and version control. Recent policies, like the [European Health Data Space
(EHDS)](https://health.ec.europa.eu/ehealth-digital-health-and-care/european-health-data-space-regulation-ehds_en)
place additional requirements on data quality. Make sure you are
familiar with these guidelines, as compliance is mandatory and impacts
both data sharing and publication. Below we mention some key practices
for data quality.

### Data Validation

Quality checks ensure your data is complete, accurate, and consistent.

- Validate data for missing values, duplicates, and outliers.
- Use automated scripts or tools to perform regular data checks.
- Document all validation steps and corrections in internal logging methods or in files like CHANGELOG or README.

### Data Provenance and Documentation

Understanding where your data comes from and how it changes over time is critical for transparency and reproducibility.

- Record data provenance: Clearly document how data was obtained, collected, processed, and any transformations applied.
- Track data sources and versions: Note the original source, date of access, version, and any identifiers (such as a DOI or persistent link
- Link code and data: Reference the specific data version used in your analysis, so others can reproduce or verify your results.
- Use a DATA_README.md or similar file to log details about each dataset, including file descriptions, formats, and any important caveats.

### Version Control

Version control is essential for reproducibility and collaboration. While
Git is the best tool for tracking changes to your code, scripts, and
documentation, it is not well-suited for managing large datasets or
binary data.

- Use Git to track your analysis scripts, notebooks, configuration files, and documentation.
- Commit changes regularly with clear, descriptive messages.
- Maintain a CHANGELOG file to record significant updates or corrections to your code or analysis.

Managing data files:

- For small, text-based datasets (e.g., small CSVs): you can version these in Git, but keep them minimal.
- For larger datasets or binary files:
  - Do not store large data files directly in Git. This can quickly bloat your repository and slow down collaboration.
Instead, use:
  - Data repositories (e.g., Zenodo, Figshare, or similar for published public data).
  - Cloud storage (e.g., Surfdrive, Nextcloud, or a dedicated data server).
  - Git LFS (Large File Storage) for versioning data files if your workflow requires it, but be aware of storage limits and setup requirements.
- Always document the source, version, and location of your data in your repository (e.g., in the README.md).

**Tip**: Always keep your data and code management separate, but
well-documented and linked. This makes your research more transparent
and reproducible.

## Data Sharing and Access

### Internal Sharing

Share data securely with colleagues using approved RIVM platforms.

- Set permissions thoughtfully, giving access only to those who need it.
- Regularly remove unnecessary or outdated files from shared folders.
- Remove or (pseudo)anonymise any personal or sensitive information before sharing.
- Clearly document which data is shared, who the recipients are, and under what conditions or agreements the sharing takes place.

### External Sharing

When sharing data outside the organization, follow your institutes policies in addition to the internal sharing tips.

- Use data repositories for data publication en code repositories for code publication, following institute, funder or journal requirements.
- Use SUrf research drive or Surfdrive for external data transfer.
- If sharing data openly, specify the applicable open license (such as CC-BY or CC0) and ensure users understand any restrictions or requirements.

## Data Archiving and Long-term Preservation

### Archiving 🗄️

Archive final datasets and documentation using approved systems. 

- Discuss how to ensure long-term storage and when archiving will take place.
- Ensure metadata and documentation are complete and accurate.
- Mark datasets as final and ready for archiving when needed.
- Keep in mind that metadata should be preserved permanently, even if datasets are deleted.
